newsitem.title: CENTRAL AFRICAN REPUBLIC: Mutineers consider Central African peace plan.
newsitem.headline: Mutineers consider Central African peace plan.

text.p: Army mutineers in the Central African Republic put off a meeting with African mediators on Monday saying they needed more time to prepare their response to a blueprint for peace in the impoverished nation.

"We were not able to meet the African mediating team this morning because we were finalising our position ahead of the meeting," the mutineer's French-trained spokesman, Lieutenant Parfait Mbay, told Reuters.

He said the meeting, to discuss the mutineers' role under the plan to end the former French colony's third army mutinty in under a year and prevent further ethnic bloodshed, would now take place on Tuesday.
Earlier, Malian mediator General Amadou Toumani Toure told French radio that "enormous progress" had been made at talks with the mutineers on Sunday.
"So far we have had no problems and we hope that, barring problems, we should be in a position to wrap up the accords in a maximum of two or three days," he said.
The peace blueprint, thrashed out last week during all-party round-table talks, calls for a national unity government open to all parties and representatives of society at large.
It also calls for the despatch of African peacekeepers and an amnesty for all involved in the mutiny.

French troops, based in the country under a defence pact, patrol the capital Bangui and form a buffer between mutineers and their foes in the presidential guard. France has welcomed the idea of using African peacekeepers.
Mutinies in April and May began over pay and conditions but turned into a campaign to oust Ange-Felix Patasse, a northern civilian politician who won presidential elections in 1993.
The latest mutiny, which began on November 15, degenerated into ethnic feuding. The death toll runs into hundreds.
A truce between army loyalists and the mutineers, mainly minority Yakomas from the same southern tribe as former military leader Andre Kolingba, expires on January 23.
Toumani Toure told a ceremony closing the round-table talks he would brief the presidents of Chad, Gabon, Burkina Faso and Mali and ask them to come to Bangui to sign the peace plan.
The four presidents visited Bangui to launch the mediation at the request of a Franco-African summit in Burkina Faso in December.
Toumani Toure, who toppled Mali's former dictator Moussa Traore in 1991, is widely respected for the way he ushered in democracy in Mali a year later and then stepped down.

The Central African Republic hit world headlines in the 1970s with the extravagent rule of self-proclaimed emperor Jean-Bedel Bokassa, who was toppled in a French-backed coup in 1979 and died last year.
